text: The science of sleep has advanced rapidly in the past two decades. Researchers now know that during deep sleep the brain consolidates memories and clears metabolic _______(1). Sleep deprivation, even partial, impairs attention, slows reaction time and weakens the immune _______(2). Chronic shortage is also linked to obesity, diabetes and cardiovascular _______(3), which is why public-health agencies treat insufficient sleep as a serious _______(4).
explanation: Answers: waste (metabolic waste is cleared during deep sleep), system (the immune system weakens), disease (cardiovascular disease), problem (a serious public-health problem). The distractors do not fit: glucose is a sugar, muscle belongs to the locomotor system, weather and vacation do not collocate with the gaps.
trap: Test the collocation, not the topic: 'metabolic waste', 'immune system' and 'public-health problem' are fixed pairs. Distractors are plausible nouns from a related field.

text: Coral reefs occupy less than one percent of the ocean floor, yet they support roughly a quarter of all marine _______(1). Rising sea temperatures cause corals to expel the algae living in their tissues, a phenomenon called bleaching; without those algae the coral loses both its color and its principal _______(2) of energy. Local threats such as pollution and overfishing compound the _______(3), but curbing emissions remains the single most effective protection, according to marine _______(4).
explanation: Answers: species (a quarter of marine species), source (the principal source of energy), damage (compound the damage), biologists (according to marine biologists). Drought, cargo, rainfall and tourists are related to the topic but collocate with none of the gaps.
trap: Two gaps follow familiar frames: 'source of energy' and 'according to biologists'. Read the whole sentence before choosing — several bank words look topical.

text: Central banks influence the economy mainly by setting short-term interest _______(1). When inflation rises above target, policymakers typically raise rates to cool demand: borrowing becomes more _______(2), saving becomes more attractive, and spending on homes and durable goods slows. The instrument is blunt, however; tightening too far can tip the economy into _______(3), while acting too late allows price increases to become _______(4) in wage demands and expectations.
explanation: Answers: rates (interest rates), expensive (borrowing becomes more expensive), recession (tip the economy into recession), entrenched (price increases become entrenched). Taxes, affordable, prosperity and temporary contradict or fail to complete the frames.
trap: The pairs 'interest rates' and 'tip the economy into recession' are fixed collocations; 'entrenched' is the only word that completes 'become ___ in wage demands'.

text: Vaccination trains the immune system to recognize a pathogen without causing the illness itself. A vaccine introduces a harmless fragment or inactivated form of the virus, prompting the body to produce _______(1) that remain in circulation for years. When enough of a community is protected, transmission chains break down — a phenomenon known as herd _______(2) — which shields people who cannot be vaccinated for medical _______(3). Outbreaks reappear wherever coverage drops, as measles resurgences in several countries have _______(4).
explanation: Answers: antibodies (the body produces antibodies), immunity (herd immunity), reasons (for medical reasons), shown (have shown, present perfect). Bacteria, quarantine, habits and promised do not complete the frames.
trap: 'Herd immunity' and 'for medical reasons' are fixed expressions; the last gap needs a past participle agreeing with 'have'.

text: Cities that have prioritized walking and cycling report measurable gains in public health and in local commerce. Wide sidewalks, protected bike lanes and reliable public transport reduce dependence on private vehicles, cutting both congestion and emissions. Street trees and green corridors also lower summer temperatures and soften traffic noise, which makes dense neighborhoods more _______(1) to live in. Critics point to the _______(2) of building such infrastructure, but evaluations usually find that the benefits — fewer crashes, healthier residents, higher _______(3) for street-level shops — outweigh the expense, which is why planners increasingly treat space for people, not vehicles, as the _______(4) of good urban design.
explanation: Answers: attractive (more attractive to live in), cost (the cost of building), revenue (higher revenue for shops), benchmark (the benchmark of good urban design). Parking, rent, ceiling and obstacle do not complete the frames.
trap: The last gap is abstract: 'the ___ of good urban design' calls for a standard-setting noun, not a physical one.

text: Most plastic entering the ocean does not stay on the surface for long. Sunlight and waves break items into ever smaller fragments, called microplastics, which are ingested by plankton, shellfish and fish — and therefore travel up the food _______(1), including to humans. Because no single nation owns the open ocean, cleanup depends on international _______(2), which move slowly. The most effective measures are upstream: banning single-use items, improving waste _______(3) and making producers responsible for packaging — policies that several coastal countries have already _______(4).
explanation: Answers: chain (food chain), agreements (international agreements), collection (waste collection), adopted (have adopted, present perfect). Market, borders, disposal and ignored fail to complete the frames — 'disposal' tempts in gap 3, but the text already names waste collection as the measure.
trap: Watch the verb frame in the last gap: 'have ___' demands a past participle, and the sentence is positive (policies adopted, not ignored).

text: Students often reread notes and highlight passages, yet research shows these techniques are among the least effective ways to learn. Retrieval practice — answering questions from memory — and spaced repetition, which spreads study over days, produce far greater _______(1) for the same time invested. The advantage appears across ages and subjects, from vocabulary to mathematics, suggesting the effect reflects how memory itself is _______(2). Cramming can still pass tomorrow's quiz, but the knowledge fades within weeks, whereas spaced study builds _______(3) that lasts, a distinction teachers now emphasize in _______(4) development programs.
explanation: Answers: retention (greater retention), organized (how memory is organized), durability (builds durability that lasts), training (teacher training programs). Attention, printed, difficulty and hiring do not complete the frames.
trap: Gap 2 follows a passive frame ('memory is ___'), which rules out nouns; gap 4 needs the noun that pairs with 'development programs'.

text: Volcanoes are not merely destructive. Eruptive ash weathers into some of the world's most fertile soil, which is why farming communities have long _______(1) on volcanic slopes. Geothermal energy taps the heat beneath such regions, providing reliable electricity with low _______(2). And over geological time, volcanic gases helped build the atmosphere and the oceans, seeding the conditions that made life _______(3). The hazard is real — eruptions near populated areas demand careful monitoring and evacuation _______(4) — but much of the planet's surface is the work of volcanism.
explanation: Answers: settled (have settled on volcanic slopes), emissions (electricity with low emissions), possible (made life possible), plans (evacuation plans). Competed, salaries, profitable and laws do not complete the frames.
trap: Collocation rules here: 'settle on slopes', 'low emissions', 'made life possible' and 'evacuation plans' are the only grammatical and semantic fits.
